title: Polylogarithmic maintenance of the exact global minimum cut
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized data structure maintaining the exact global minimum-cut value of a fully dynamic simple unweighted undirected graph with polylogarithmic expected amortized update time, polylogarithmic worst-case query time and polynomial space? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) and fixed integers \(b\ge1,c\ge0\) such that, for every fixed integer confidence parameter \(a\ge1\), there is a constant \(C_a\ge1\) for which the following holds? For every \(n\ge2\), initialize on the empty graph on \([n]\). For every legal operation sequence \(\sigma\) fixed independently of the random bits, with \(U\) updates and \(Q\) queries and \(U+Q\le n^a\), require all of:
\[\text{space on every execution}\le C_a n^b\text{ words},\qquad \mathbb E[T_{\rm init}+T_{\rm updates}]\le C_a\bigl(n^b+U L^c\bigr),\]
\[\text{each query takes at most }C_aL^c\text{ steps on every execution},\qquad \Pr[\text{all }Q\text{ answers equal the current }\lambda(G)]\ge1-n^{-3},\]
where \(L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) and the machine model and costs are defined below. The exponents \(b,c\) and program are independent of \(a,n,\sigma\) and all cut values; constants may depend on \(a\).
definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), fixed throughout the sequence. Each edge is an unordered pair \(\{u,v\}\) of distinct vertices and occurs at most once. A legal update inserts an absent edge or deletes a present edge. There are no loops, weights, parallel edges or vertex changes. For \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq[n]\), put \(\delta_G(S)=\{\{u,v\}\in E(G):|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}\) and
\[\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq[n]}|\delta_G(S)|.\]
Thus \(0\le\lambda(G)\le n-1\), and \(\lambda(G)=0\) precisely for disconnected graphs, including the initial empty graph. A query returns just this integer, not a minimizing vertex set, edge list or prescribed-terminal cut. Isolated vertices are not discarded. There is no upper bound on connectivity other than \(n-1\).

The algorithm receives \(n\) and \(a\) at initialization. It then receives one operation at a time, represented by a query tag or an insertion/deletion tag with the two vertex indices. It is not given future operations. The external sequence is fixed in advance independently of the algorithm’s randomness, including any answers or internal state; its prefixes are legal. Correctness is simultaneous over all queries in each fixed sequence, not simultaneous over all possible sequences for one random seed. No correctness obligation is imposed on invalid update sequences. Initialization and updates must finish almost surely before the next operation is provided; the finite expectation bound applies to every legal sequence and hence to each prefix. Queries have the stated worst-case bound for every choice of random bits. Expected cost includes unsuccessful executions, not only those with correct answers.

Use a uniform word-RAM. For each fixed \(a\), the word length is \(w=B(a)L\) bits, where \(B(a)\ge1\) is an integer determined by a fixed computable function chosen with the algorithm, independently of \(n\) and the operations. Words represent unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). One step may read or write a word at a word-sized address, copy a word, compare two words, branch, apply a bitwise Boolean operation, shift, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or perform unsigned integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. A random instruction returns one fresh independent uniformly distributed \(w\)-bit word in one step. Arithmetic requiring more than one word is charged for its word operations; there are no real-number, unbounded-integer or oracle primitives. The finite program and computable word-length rule are common to all inputs, with no nonuniform advice or free precomputed tables.

Space counts all stored words, including tables and temporary work. Initialization work, random choices, rebuilding and all other computation belong to the operation during which they occur; there is no uncharged background work. The expectation bound includes initialization once and all update work. Query work is separately bounded, so expected total time is also at most \(C_a(n^b+(U+Q)L^c)\). The additive initialization allowance is polynomial, not an allowance repeated at each update. Amortization concerns the total over the supplied sequence, with no average over random input graphs. A query answer that differs from the exact integer is an error. The fixed failure bound \(n^{-3}\) applies to the entire sequence of length at most \(n^a\); \(a\) is supplied to set the horizon and confidence, not to reveal the actual sequence.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of a data structure satisfying every displayed requirement, or an unconditional proof of the negation in the same model. A positive answer must define one program and its computable word-length rule, establish fixed exponents, and prove the space, expected total update/initialization cost, worst-case query cost and joint correctness probability for every allowed parameter and oblivious sequence. A negative answer must rule out every such choice of program and exponents; a theorem conditional on a conjecture alone does not do so. An insertion-only algorithm, an approximation, a bounded-connectivity guarantee, superpolylogarithmic update time, or polylogarithmic updates accompanied by slower queries is insufficient. Lower bounds for weighted graphs or terminal cuts require a proved transfer preserving this exact model. The output is exact because the question asks for an exact-maintenance algorithm; there is no additive 1/100 approximation option.
why: A central exact dynamic graph problem asking whether a global measure of edge connectivity can be updated as efficiently as basic connectivity, across the full range of cut values.

importance.reason: A fundamental data-structure question with a persistent gap between incremental, approximate and exact fully dynamic algorithms; common terminal-cut lower bounds do not settle it.

progress.text: The OMv framework leaves polylogarithmic dynamic global minimum cut as an explicit open problem in §5.2.
Goranci–Henzinger–Thorup achieve exact polylogarithmic incremental maintenance, allowing insertions only.
Goranci and coauthors give exact fully dynamic algorithms for unrestricted edge connectivity; v2 corrects an expander-decomposition runtime.
El-Hayek–Henzinger–Li obtain \((1+o(1))\)-approximate fully dynamic minimum cut in subpolynomial amortized time.
El-Hayek–Henzinger–Li obtain deterministic exact subpolynomial amortized updates for superpolylogarithmic, but still restricted, cut sizes.
Kenneth-Mordoch–Krauthgamer’s SOSA paper gives simpler exact algorithms and a connectivity-dependent update/query tradeoff.
The revised pseudo-deterministic minimum-cut preprint gives polylogarithmic updates with nearly linear queries, a different resource guarantee.
The final Algorithmica Theorem 6 gives deterministic exact amortized update time \(\widetilde O(\min\{m^{11/12},m^{11/13}n^{1/13},n^{3/2}\})\) for simple graphs.

status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No algorithm satisfying both polylogarithmic expected-amortized updates and worst-case value queries for unrestricted exact connectivity, or unconditional impossibility theorem in the chosen model, was found in the bounded primary-source review. The SODA2026 exact result restricts cut size; the final June2026 tree-packing bound is not polylogarithmic. The February2026 pseudo-deterministic result has nearly linear queries, and the SOSA2026 tradeoff depends on connectivity. These are distinct guarantees; new proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: The global minimum cut measures the weakest separation anywhere in a network: how many edges must fail before some nonempty part separates from the rest. Maintaining this number as individual links appear and disappear is a natural extension of dynamic connectivity. Connectivity only distinguishes \(\lambda =0\) from \(\lambda \ge 1\); the present question requires the exact integer throughout its full range from zero to \(n- 1\).

A small update need not make the identity of the best cut easy to maintain. For example, two dense clusters joined by a few edges have a global cut determined by their interface, although every individual vertex can have high degree. As the interface changes, an unrelated part of the graph can become the weakest separation. Tracking vertex degrees alone therefore does not identify the optimum.

The value changes by at most one after a single edge insertion or deletion: each individual cut changes by at most one, and taking the minimum preserves that bound. Stability of the value alone does not specify whether an update changes it. The all-input guarantee includes long sequences in which different vertex partitions attain the minimum.

The card requests a number, allowing a polylogarithmic query bound without an output-size obstruction. Listing the edges of a large minimum cut or all vertices on one side can require linear time merely to write the answer. It also uses the ordinary global convention \(\lambda =0\) for disconnected graphs. The inherited 2026 algorithm uses minimum proper, nonzero cuts internally; those intermediate objects are not the definition of this card’s output.

Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai and Saranurak’s OMv paper explicitly identifies dynamic minimum cut as an unresolved frontier for polylogarithmic updates. Its many conditional lower bounds do not automatically transfer to this task. A minimum s–t cut must separate prescribed terminals, whereas a global minimum cut may isolate a completely different region. A reduction has to preserve that freedom, not silently introduce terminal constraints.

Goranci, Henzinger and Thorup give a deterministic algorithm with polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant query time for exact incremental minimum cut. Its permitted updates only insert edges. The present target permits both insertions and deletions, including repeated removal and reinsertion of the same edge.

For unrestricted cut values in simple graphs, Goranci and coauthors give a randomized exact algorithm with \(\widetilde O(n)\) worst-case update time and a deterministic algorithm with \(\widetilde O(m^{29/31}n^{1/31})\) amortized time. Their March 2024 revision corrects an expander-decomposition running time. These bounds are substantial improvements over recomputing from scratch, but do not give the requested polylogarithmic guarantee. Here \(m\) denotes the current edge count and \(\widetilde O\) hides logarithmic factors.

The final June 2026 Algorithmica article by de Vos and Christiansen gives the deterministic exact amortized bound \(\widetilde O(\min\{m^{11/12},m^{11/13}n^{1/13},n^{3/2}\})\) for simple unweighted graphs. This is Theorem 6 in the journal version; the article distinguishes it from an erroneous earlier cited exponent. Returning a full cut has a separate output-sensitive bound. The theorem does not establish polylogarithmic maintenance for all graph densities.

The inherited SODA 2026 theorem of El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li gives deterministic exact \(n^{o(1)}\) amortized update time within a cut-size range bounded by \(2^{\Theta((\log n)^{3/4-\eta})}\), for fixed \(0<\eta<3/4\) in its parameter regime. It extends the earlier small-connectivity range. Both restrictions matter: the theorem does not cover every value up to \(n-1\), and a subpolynomial time bound need not be a fixed power of \(\log n\).

The word “subpolynomial” permits bounds that are larger than every polylogarithm; for example, \(2^{\sqrt{\log_2 n}}=n^{o(1)}\) eventually exceeds \((\log_2 n)^c\) for every fixed \(c\). Thus replacing “polylogarithmic” by “subpolynomial” would change the target even if exactness and the cut-size range were otherwise identical.

El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li’s SODA 2025 algorithm instead maintains a \((1+o(1))\)-approximate global cut in subpolynomial amortized time without a small-cut promise. A multiplicative estimate with relative error \(\epsilon\) can have additive error \(\epsilon\lambda\). Integrality does not turn such a guarantee into exactness uniformly over large \(\lambda\); the approximation accuracy and its effect on running time remain essential.

Kenneth-Mordoch’s February 2026 preprint reports a canonical exact minimum-cut algorithm with polylogarithmic worst-case updates and \(\widetilde O(n)\) queries. Its query procedure constructs a sparse contracted graph and computes a cut on that graph before reporting the result. Consequently, its stated query bound is not just the cost of printing the cut’s vertices, and the theorem does not provide the polylogarithmic value query required here.

The SOSA 2026 paper by Kenneth-Mordoch and Krauthgamer gives another tradeoff: its publisher abstract states \(\widetilde O(n/\lambda)\) worst-case updates and \(\widetilde O(n^2/\lambda^2)\) worst-case queries for positive connectivity. This becomes efficient in the high-connectivity range, but it is not a polylogarithmic bound uniform over all positive values of \(\lambda\). Disconnected graphs are also part of the present target.

The remaining question isolates two bottlenecks at once: exactness for unrestricted connectivity and polylogarithmic update cost. Randomization and amortization are allowed to make it a broad algorithmic target. A positive result would put a numerical global resilience measure close to the cost of maintaining basic connectivity, while a suitable lower bound would explain why this more detailed information requires fundamentally more work.

sentences: The global minimum cut is the minimum number of edges crossing any nonempty proper vertex subset, with value zero for a disconnected graph.
The question asks for one randomized data structure returning that exact value while arbitrary legal edge insertions and deletions arrive online.
It requires polylogarithmic expected amortized updates, polylogarithmic worst-case queries and polynomial space, with explicit initialization cost and uniform exponents.
For each fixed oblivious polynomial-length operation sequence, all answers must be simultaneously correct with error probability at most \(n^{-3}\).
A complete Lean proof must establish the whole guarantee or its unconditional impossibility; approximate, small-cut, insertion-only and fast-update/slow-query results do not suffice.

source_formulation.text: Retains the polylogarithmic exact fully dynamic global-minimum-cut question from the OMv open-problem discussion, using the previously selected simple unweighted, expected-amortized Monte Carlo convention. Makes the inherited polynomial horizon, common exponents, polynomial initialization/space, worst-case value queries and oblivious-sequence joint correctness explicit. The specified RAM instructions and integer confidence parameter fix the model; no weighted, terminal-cut or small-connectivity variant is substituted.
